section.title: Justice and the Three Feasts
section.sectionRationale: This chapter closes the Book of the Covenant's case law with two further movements: courtroom integrity that refuses to bend for either the powerful or the poor, and a calendar of rest and feasting that structures Israel's whole year around trust in God's provision.
section.thesis: The LORD demands impartial justice that neither follows the crowd nor favors the poor out of misplaced sympathy, commands a sabbatical year and weekly Sabbath rest for the sake of the poor and the land, and fixes three annual feasts that bring all Israel's males before Him in thanksgiving for His provision.
section.frameNote: Three movements: laws of courtroom and neighborly integrity, refusing false witness, bribery, and partiality in either direction; the sabbatical year and weekly Sabbath for land, servant, and animal alike; and the three annual pilgrimage feasts that anchor Israel's calendar in gratitude.

units.label: Impartial justice
units.note: neither crowd nor bribe nor favoritism

verses.text: “You shall not spread a false report. Do not join the wicked by being a malicious witness.
You shall not follow the crowd in wrongdoing. When you testify in a lawsuit, do not pervert justice by siding with the crowd.
And do not show favoritism to a poor man in his lawsuit.
If you encounter your enemy's stray ox or donkey, you must return it to him.
If you see the donkey of one who hates you fallen under its load, do not leave it there; you must help him with it.
You shall not deny {{justice|justice}} to the poor in their lawsuits.
Stay far away from a false accusation. Do not kill the innocent or the just, for I will not acquit the guilty.
Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous.
Do not oppress a foreign resident, since you yourselves know how it feels to be foreigners; for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.

units.label: The sabbatical year and Sabbath day
units.note: rest for the land, the poor, and the servant

verses.text: For six years you are to sow your land and gather its produce,

but in the {{seventh|seventh}} year you must let it rest and lie fallow, so that the poor among your people may eat from the field and the wild animals may consume what they leave. Do the same with your vineyard and olive grove.

For six days you are to do your work, but on the seventh day you must cease, so that your ox and your donkey may rest and the son of your maidservant may be refreshed, as well as the foreign resident.
Pay close attention to everything I have said to you. You must not invoke the names of other gods; they must not be heard on your lips.

units.label: Three annual feasts
units.note: no one appears before Me empty-handed

verses.text: Three times a year you are to celebrate a {{feast|feast}} to Me.

You are to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread as I commanded you: At the appointed time in the month of Abib you are to eat unleavened bread for seven days, because that was the month you came out of Egypt. No one may appear before Me empty-handed.

You are also to keep the Feast of Harvest with the firstfruits of the produce from what you sow in the field. 
And keep the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year, when you gather your produce from the field.
Three times a year all your males are to appear before the Lord GOD.
You must not offer the blood of My sacrifices with anything leavened, nor may the fat of My feast remain until morning.

Bring the best of the firstfruits of your soil to the house of the LORD your God. 
You must not cook a young goat in its mother's milk.

justice.gloss: Justice, judgment, the right ordering of a legal case. This chapter insists mishpat must never bend, not toward the powerful through bribery, not toward the poor through misplaced sympathy, but must follow truth alone.

seventh.gloss: Release, the letting-go of the land every seventh year. The word shares its root with the release of debts later commanded in Deuteronomy 15, tying agricultural rest to a wider pattern of periodic release built into Israel's calendar.

feast.gloss: A pilgrimage feast, a festival marked by joyful gathering and travel to worship. Three times a year Israel's men were to leave their fields and travel to appear before the LORD, structuring the whole agricultural calendar around gratitude.

basic.context: This chapter closes Israel's early case law with instructions for honest courts, refusing bribes and favoritism in either direction, then moves into rhythms of rest, a sabbatical year for the land and a weekly Sabbath, and three annual feasts that bring the whole nation together to thank God for His provision.
basic.hermeneutics: These are specific instructions for Israel's ancient courts, agricultural calendar, and worship life under the old covenant. They are not direct legislation for modern courts or farming practices, but they reveal enduring principles: impartial justice, rest built into work, and gratitude structured into the rhythm of life, all fulfilled and carried forward under the new covenant.
basic.originalLanguages: Israel's mishpat, justice, must never bend for bribe or crowd or misplaced sympathy for the poor; it must simply be true. The shemittah, the seventh-year release of the land, builds rest for the poor and the earth itself into the calendar. And three times a year Israel gathers for a chag, a joyful pilgrimage feast, before the LORD.
basic.typology: The Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Harvest, and the Feast of Ingathering trace the whole shape of redemption, deliverance, firstfruits, and final harvest, a pattern the New Testament reads as fulfilled in Christ's death, resurrection, and the final ingathering of all nations.
basic.christ: Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb and describes His resurrection as the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Corinthians 15:20, directly picking up the imagery of these very feasts; and the command against cooking a young goat in its mother's milk has long been read as protecting the boundary between life-giving nourishment and death, a boundary Christ crosses only to give life, never to bring death.
basic.god: God cares as much about courtroom integrity as He does about worship, refusing to let either the powerful or the poor manipulate justice, and He builds mercy and rest directly into Israel's economic calendar, insisting that even the land and the animals share in Sabbath rest. His holiness and His practical compassion are inseparable.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 calls Christ's resurrection the firstfruits, echoing the Feast of Harvest. Leviticus 25:1-7 expands the sabbatical year into the fuller Sabbath and Jubilee system. James 2:1-9 warns against partiality in judgment, echoing this chapter's insistence on impartial justice.
basic.oneStory: God insists on justice that bends for no one and builds rest and gratitude into the very rhythm of Israel's year. This pattern of impartial justice, rest, and thanksgiving before God carries through the whole Bible and finds its fulfillment in Christ, our Passover and our firstfruits, who secures the final, great ingathering of every nation.

context.literary:
Exodus 23:1-19 brings the case laws of the Book of the Covenant to a close and begins to turn the whole collection back toward worship, where it started in 20:22-26. The form is almost entirely direct command, "You shall not... you must...," rather than the "if a man" cases of chapters 21 and 22.

Verses 1 to 9 are carefully built. The outer verses deal with the courtroom: false reports, malicious witnesses, the crowd and the poor litigant in verses 1 to 3; the poor, the false charge, the innocent and the bribe in verses 6 to 8. In the middle, verses 4 and 5, the law suddenly steps out of the court and onto the road, to an enemy's stray ox and a hater's fallen donkey. The placement is pointed. The person you meet as an opponent in court is the same person whose animal you must rescue on the way home. The unit closes, verse 9, by repeating almost word for word the foreigner law of Exodus 22:21, framing the whole section of social law with the memory of Egypt.

Verses 10 to 12 form a pair built on the number seven: six years of sowing and a seventh of rest for the land, six days of work and a seventh day of rest for animals, servants and foreigners. Verse 13 is a hinge. It summarises ("Pay close attention to everything I have said to you") and forbids even speaking the names of other gods, preparing for the calendar that follows.

Verses 14 to 17 set out the three pilgrimage feasts, enclosed by two parallel lines, "Three times a year," verses 14 and 17. Verses 18 and 19 then add four short rules about sacrifice and firstfruits, ending with the enigmatic command about a young goat. Almost the same calendar and the same four rules reappear in Exodus 34:18-26 when the covenant is renewed after the golden calf, which shows how central they were.
context.historical:
Israel's legal system was local and lay. Cases were heard by elders at the town gate, and verdicts often depended on witnesses rather than on physical evidence. A single false witness, or a group of them, could decide a man's life, which is why the law insists elsewhere on at least two witnesses and punishes a false witness with the penalty he sought for his neighbour, Deuteronomy 19:16-19. Bribery was a constant danger in the ancient world, and the prophets repeatedly name it as the rot of Israel's courts; even Samuel's sons "turned aside toward dishonest gain, accepting bribes and perverting justice," 1 Samuel 8:3.

The agricultural year stands behind the rest of the passage. The Feast of Unleavened Bread fell in Abib, the first month, in early spring, at the start of the barley harvest, and it was tied to the Passover and the exodus, as the footnote notes. The Feast of Harvest, later called the Feast of Weeks or Pentecost, marked the wheat harvest in late spring. The Feast of Ingathering, later the Feast of Tabernacles, came in the autumn after the grapes and olives had been gathered, "at the end of the year," that is, the end of the agricultural cycle. At each feast the men of Israel were to appear before the LORD at His sanctuary, and none was to come empty-handed.

The sabbatical year was a bold demand in a subsistence economy. Leaving land unsown for a year required trust that the sixth year's harvest and the land's volunteer growth would carry the family through. The fallow year also served the poor, who could glean freely, and even the wild animals. Later Scripture suggests Israel neglected it; the Chronicler describes the exile as the land finally enjoying "its Sabbath rest," 2 Chronicles 36:21.

The weekly Sabbath of verse 12 is framed not by creation, as in Exodus 20:11, but by mercy for animals, the son of a maidservant and the foreigner. In a world where the poorest labourers were never given rest, this was radical.
context.canonical:
The laws of courtroom integrity are developed throughout Scripture. Leviticus 19:15 restates verse 3 and verse 6 together: "you must not show partiality to the poor or favoritism to the rich; you are to judge your neighbor fairly." Deuteronomy 16:19 repeats the bribery clause almost word for word. The law of the enemy's animal is expanded to the neighbour's lost ox, sheep and cloak in Deuteronomy 22:1-4, and it stands behind Proverbs 25:21-22, which Paul quotes in Romans 12:20: "If your enemy is hungry, feed him."

The sabbatical year is developed in Leviticus 25:2-7, where the land itself keeps "a Sabbath to the LORD," and in Deuteronomy 15:1-2, where the seventh year also becomes a year for cancelling debts. Nehemiah's community pledged, "Every seventh year we will let the fields lie fallow," Nehemiah 10:31, and 2 Chronicles 36:21 reads the exile as its enforced keeping.

The three feasts are listed again in Exodus 34:18-26, Leviticus 23, Numbers 28 to 29 and Deuteronomy 16:1-17. The Gospels set the climax of Jesus' ministry at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, Luke 22:1; Paul calls Christ "our Passover lamb" and urges the church to keep the feast "with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth," 1 Corinthians 5:7-8. The Spirit was poured out on the Feast of Harvest, Pentecost, Acts 2:1, and about three thousand were gathered that day, Acts 2:41. At the Feast of Tabernacles Jesus stood and cried, "If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink," John 7:37. Zechariah 14:16 foresees the nations going up year after year to keep that same feast.

At the trial of Jesus the very sins of verses 1 and 2 are committed: "many bore false witness against Jesus," Mark 14:56, and Pilate yielded to the crowd, "their clamor prevailed," Luke 23:23.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to understand that justice is a form of worship. The same God who calls His people to His feasts demands truth in their testimony and fairness in their verdicts, and verse 7 roots it in His own character: "I will not acquit the guilty." A court that bends for a crowd, a bribe or a sympathetic story is misrepresenting the God in whose name it judges.

He also wanted them to see that love reaches enemies. The stray ox and the fallen donkey of verses 4 and 5 are set in the middle of courtroom law so that Israel could not confine justice to formal proceedings. Doing right by a man you are suing is part of the same obedience.

Then the passage teaches that time itself belongs to God. The seventh day, the seventh year and the three feasts built rest, generosity and gratitude into the calendar. Israel would not drift into thankfulness; the calendar would take them there. Every spring and autumn the whole nation would be reminded that the harvest was a gift and that the God who gave it had brought them out of Egypt. The rule that no one may appear before Him empty-handed was meant to teach that gratitude is expressed, not merely felt.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These were binding laws for Israel's courts, fields and festivals. The specific forms, the sabbatical fallow, three pilgrimages to the sanctuary, the rules about leaven and fat, belonged to Israel's life in the land under the Sinai covenant. The New Testament does not require Christians to keep Israel's festival calendar; Paul warns against letting anyone judge believers "with regard to a feast," since these were "a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ," Colossians 2:16-17.

The moral commands of verses 1 to 9 are another matter. False witness, bribery, partiality and hostility to the foreigner are condemned in the New Testament as firmly as in the Old, James 2:1-4. The command to help an enemy's animal is surpassed by Jesus' command to love the enemy himself, Matthew 5:44. And the principle behind the calendar, that rest and worship must be built into the rhythm of life rather than left to chance, remains wise and good. The church gathers weekly on the Lord's Day, celebrates Christ our Passover, and gives the firstfruits of its income, applying these patterns in the light of their fulfilment.

debates.question: Does verse 3's warning against favoring the poor in a lawsuit conflict with the Bible's frequent concern for the poor elsewhere?

views.label: No conflict, different contexts
views.case: Elsewhere Scripture commands generosity, care, and justice for the poor precisely because they are otherwise vulnerable to exploitation, Exodus 22:21-27; this verse addresses a courtroom specifically, warning that even good sympathy must not corrupt a judge's factual determination of guilt or innocence.

views.label: A necessary balancing corrective
views.case: Some read this verse as a deliberate check against a well-intentioned but real danger, that judges moved by compassion might excuse actual wrongdoing by a poor litigant, undermining the very justice system that protects the poor in the first place.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree: true justice requires impartiality toward all litigants regardless of social status, which is itself what ultimately protects the poor from arbitrary rulings in either direction.

debates.question: Why does verse 19 forbid cooking a young goat in its mother's milk?

views.label: A rejection of a pagan practice
views.case: An older and once popular view connected the command to a Canaanite ritual, citing a text from ancient Ugarit that was read as describing a kid cooked in milk. The command's placement among rules of worship and harvest fits this. However, the reading of that Ugaritic text has since been widely questioned, so this view now rests on less secure ground than it once did.

views.label: A lesson in reverence for life and the order of creation
views.case: Milk is the food God gave to sustain the young. To use a mother's milk to cook her own offspring turns what nourishes life into a means of death. The law elsewhere shows similar concern: an animal must stay with its mother seven days, Exodus 22:30 and Leviticus 22:27, and a mother bird may not be taken with her young, Deuteronomy 22:6-7. On this reading the command teaches Israel to honour the bonds God built into creation.

views.label: A boundary expanded by later Jewish practice
views.case: Rabbinic tradition, noting that the command appears three times, Exodus 23:19, 34:26 and Deuteronomy 14:21, built on it the complete separation of meat and dairy in Jewish dietary law. That practice goes well beyond the text's own wording but shows how seriously the command was taken.

debates.bearing: The text gives no reason, so certainty is not possible. The second view has the strongest support from within the Law itself, which repeatedly guards the bond between a mother animal and her young. Whatever its origin, the command stands among the firstfruits laws as a reminder that holiness touches even the kitchen.

study.originalLanguages:
The "false report" of verse 1 is shema shav, literally "an empty hearing," a rumour with nothing behind it. Shav is the word of the third commandment, "You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain," Exodus 20:7, and Deuteronomy 5:20 uses it for the "false" witness of the ninth. The "malicious witness" is literally an ed chamas, "a witness of violence," using the word for the violence that filled the earth before the flood, Genesis 6:11. Lying testimony is not merely inaccurate; it is an act of violence against a neighbour. Psalm 35:11 uses the same phrase for the "hostile witnesses" who rise against the psalmist.

Verse 2 turns on one verb used three times, natah, to bend or turn aside: "do not turn aside after the many to bend justice." The same verb returns in verse 6, "You shall not deny justice," literally "bend the justice" of the poor. Justice is pictured as a straight line that the crowd, the bribe or the judge's sympathy tries to bend. "The crowd" is rabbim, "the many," which can mean the majority or the powerful.

Verses 3 and 6 use two different words for the poor. The one who must not be favoured in verse 3 is dal, the weak or low, and the verb "show favoritism" is hadar, to honour or adorn, the word used of splendour and majesty. Even adorning the poor man's case is forbidden. The one whose justice must not be bent in verse 6 is evyon, the needy, the same word as "the poor among your people" in verse 11. Leviticus 19:15 combines both sides: no partiality to the dal, no favour to the great.

In verse 7, "I will not acquit the guilty" is lo atsdiq rasha, literally "I will not declare the wicked righteous," a causative form of tsadaq. Proverbs 17:15 uses the same construction: "Acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous, both are detestable to the LORD." This is the background against which Paul makes his startling claim that God "justifies the wicked," Romans 4:5. The bribe of verse 8 is shochad, and it "blinds those who see," literally "the open-eyed," and "twists the words of the righteous."

Verse 9 contains one of the most tender phrases in the Law: "you yourselves know how it feels to be foreigners" is literally "you know the nephesh of the foreigner," his inner life, his soul. Israel knew the stranger from the inside.

The sabbatical year of verse 11 uses two verbs: shamat, "let it rest," the root behind shemittah, and natash, "lie fallow," to leave or abandon. In verse 12 the servant and foreigner "may be refreshed," yinnafesh, a verb from the same root as nephesh, to catch one's breath. Exodus 31:17 uses the same verb of God Himself: "on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed." The rest God took, He shares with the lowest worker in the household.

Verse 13 forbids Israel even to "invoke" the names of other gods, using the causative of zakar, to make remembered. It is the very form God used in 20:24, "where I cause My name to be remembered." Only one name is to be kept alive on Israel's lips.

Finally, verse 14's "three times" is shalosh regalim, literally "three feet," an idiom for "three times" that Balaam's donkey also uses, Numbers 22:28. The word for feast, chag, names a pilgrim festival, a feast kept by going up to God's appointed place. Verse 15's "empty-handed" is reqam, the word God used when He promised that Israel would not leave Egypt empty-handed, Exodus 3:21. Those who were sent out laden with gifts were never to come before Him with nothing.

typology.type: The Feast of Unleavened Bread, Exodus 23:15
typology.fulfillment: Israel ate unleavened bread for seven days to remember the haste of the exodus and the break with Egypt. Paul reads the feast through Christ: "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed," and therefore "let us keep the feast," not with old leaven but "with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth," 1 Corinthians 5:7-8. The correspondence is between a deliverance from Pharaoh and a deliverance from sin, with the old leaven now "malice and wickedness." The escalation is that the feast is no longer seven days once a year but the whole of the Christian life. The type falls short because Israel had to repeat the feast every year; the sacrifice it celebrates is now once for all.

typology.type: The Feast of Harvest and its firstfruits, Exodus 23:16
typology.fulfillment: At the first harvest Israel brought the firstfruits to God as a pledge that the whole crop was His and was coming. Paul says, "Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep," 1 Corinthians 15:20. His resurrection is the first sheaf of a harvest that guarantees the rest: "then at His coming, those who belong to Him," 15:23. The Feast of Harvest also became Pentecost, the day the Spirit was poured out and three thousand were gathered, Acts 2:1 and 2:41, and believers themselves are called "a kind of firstfruits of His creation," James 1:18. The type falls short only in scale: Israel's firstfruits were grain; Christ's are the risen body and a redeemed people.

typology.type: The Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year, Exodus 23:16
typology.fulfillment: The last feast of the agricultural year celebrated the completed harvest, when everything had been brought in. Jesus speaks of "the harvest" as "the end of the age," Matthew 13:39, and Revelation pictures the final reaping of the earth, Revelation 14:15. It was at this feast, later called Tabernacles, that Jesus offered living water to all who are thirsty, John 7:37-38, and Zechariah 14:16 sees the nations coming to keep it. John's vision of a multitude from every nation "holding palm branches," Revelation 7:9, recalls the branches of that feast, Leviticus 23:40. The escalation is from a national harvest festival to the final gathering of the redeemed from all nations.

typology.type: The seventh day and the seventh year of rest, Exodus 23:10-12
typology.fulfillment: The weekly Sabbath and the sabbatical year gave rest to people, animals and land, and released the poor to eat freely. Jesus declared that "the Sabbath was made for man," Mark 2:27, and offered Himself as its fulfilment: "Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest," Matthew 11:28. Hebrews teaches that "there remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God," Hebrews 4:9. The type falls short because Israel's rest was temporary and had to be renewed every week and every seventh year, and Israel often failed to keep it; the rest Christ gives is received by faith and will be complete in the new creation.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first through the courtroom. Its commands were broken almost to the letter at His trial. "Many bore false witness against Jesus," Mark 14:56, exactly the ed chamas of verse 1. The authorities "were seeking testimony against Jesus to put Him to death," Mark 14:55, killing "the innocent or the just," verse 7. Pilate found "no basis for a charge," Luke 23:4, yet yielded to the crowd, "their clamor prevailed," Luke 23:23, and washed his hands before them, Matthew 27:24. Verse 2's warning against siding with the many in a lawsuit describes the very failure by which the Just One was condemned.

It leads to Christ through a divine paradox. God says in verse 7, "I will not acquit the guilty." Yet the gospel announces that God "justifies the wicked," Romans 4:5. The two are reconciled only at the cross. God does not bend justice; He satisfies it. "God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God," 2 Corinthians 5:21. Isaiah saw it in advance: "My righteous Servant will justify many, and He will bear their iniquities," Isaiah 53:11. God acquits the guilty not by pretending they are innocent, but by laying their guilt on the innocent One who was wrongly condemned. The court that broke Exodus 23 became the place where God kept it.

It leads to Christ through love for enemies. Verses 4 and 5 command help for an enemy's animal. Jesus goes further: "love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you," Matthew 5:44. And He did it Himself, dying for people who were His enemies, Romans 5:10.

It leads to Christ through rest. The seventh day and seventh year gave rest to the weary and food to the poor. Jesus announced, "Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest," Matthew 11:28, and called Himself "Lord even of the Sabbath," Mark 2:28.

It leads to Christ through the feasts. He died at the Feast of Unleavened Bread as "our Passover lamb," 1 Corinthians 5:7. He rose as "the firstfruits," 1 Corinthians 15:20, and many have noted that the firstfruits sheaf was waved "on the day after the Sabbath," Leviticus 23:11, the day of His resurrection. The Spirit came at the Feast of Harvest, Acts 2:1. And at the Feast of Ingathering He invited the thirsty to come to Him and drink, John 7:37. The whole year of Israel's worship converges on one Person.

A caution: the calendar is not a secret code, and not every detail, the fat or the leaven of verse 18, needs a Christological meaning. The links here are ones the New Testament itself draws, and they rest on the main lines of the feasts: deliverance, firstfruits and final harvest.
study.god:
This passage shows a God whose justice is perfectly straight. He will not be moved by a crowd, a bribe, a sympathetic story or a powerful litigant. "I will not acquit the guilty," verse 7, is a statement about His own character, and it is why His people's courts must mirror Him. Moses says elsewhere that He is the God "showing no partiality and accepting no bribe," Deuteronomy 10:17, and Peter confesses, "God does not show favoritism," Acts 10:34. Because He judges impartially, 1 Peter 1:17, His people may never use justice as a tool of power or of pity.

He is also a God of astonishing kindness toward enemies. He commands His people to rescue the fallen donkey of the man who hates them, verse 5. The God who gives this law is the God who "is kind to the ungrateful and wicked," Luke 6:35, and who sends rain on the just and the unjust. Justice in court and kindness on the road come from the same heart.

He is a God of rest. He does not drive His creatures like Pharaoh did. He builds rest into every week and every seventh year, not only for His people but for their animals, their servants, the foreigner and even the wild beasts. The verb used for the servant's refreshment in verse 12 is the verb used of God Himself resting after creation, Exodus 31:17. God shares His own rest with the least of His creatures.

He is the God of provision and gratitude. The feasts are tied to harvests, and the command not to come empty-handed assumes that God has already filled Israel's hands. He gives first, and worship answers. That is why the firstfruits, "the best of the firstfruits," verse 19, belong to Him: not the leftovers, but the first and best, as a confession that everything comes from Him.

He is a jealous God who claims exclusive devotion. Israel may not even speak the names of other gods, verse 13, and all its feasting is to be "to Me," verse 14. The joy of the feasts is not a general celebration of the harvest but gratitude directed to the one Giver.

He is a God who remembers and wants His people to remember. The Feast of Unleavened Bread is kept "because that was the month you came out of Egypt," verse 15, and the foreigner is protected because Israel knows "the nephesh of the foreigner," verse 9. God shapes His people's hearts by giving them memories to rehearse.

For worship, this means that the God we praise on the Lord's Day is the God who watches how we testify, how we judge, how we treat our enemies, and whether we let others rest. Worship that ignores justice misrepresents Him, and justice that forgets worship loses its reason.

crossReferences.note: The Holiness Code combines verse 3 and verse 6 into one sentence: "you must not show partiality to the poor or favoritism to the rich; you are to judge your neighbor fairly." Justice leans neither up nor down. The two warnings of Exodus 23 belong together, and each guards against the danger of the other.

Moses restates the bribery clause almost exactly, "a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and twists the words of the righteous," and adds the ringing command, "Pursue justice, and justice alone, so that you may live." Integrity in court is tied to Israel's very survival in the land.

The law against the malicious witness of Exodus 23:1 is given teeth. If a witness is proven a liar, "you must do to him as he intended to do to his brother." The false witness is treated as a would-be murderer, which is exactly what the phrase "witness of violence" implies.

The law of the enemy's animal is broadened to any "brother's" lost ox, sheep, donkey or cloak, and to the animal "fallen on the road." Repeating the phrase "you must not ignore it," Moses makes the point that neighbourliness cannot be passive. Exodus 23 applies it even to one who hates you.

Paul quotes Proverbs 25:21-22, which stands in the line of Exodus 23:4-5: "If your enemy is hungry, feed him." He then draws the conclusion, "overcome evil with good." Helping an enemy's donkey was never merely about animals; it was training in the love that conquers hostility.

At Jesus' trial the Sanhedrin sought testimony to put Him to death, and "many bore false witness against Jesus," but their testimony did not agree. Every clause of Exodus 23:1-2 and 7 is broken in the condemnation of the one truly innocent man.

Paul speaks of God as the one "who justifies the wicked," using the very idea God forbade in verse 7, "I will not acquit the guilty." The tension is deliberate. God justifies the wicked not by bending justice but through Christ, who bore their guilt, so that God is both just and the justifier.

When the covenant is renewed after the golden calf, God repeats this calendar almost word for word: the three feasts, the command not to appear empty-handed, the rules on leaven and the Passover sacrifice, the firstfruits and the young goat. The repetition shows these laws were at the heart of Israel's covenant life.

Paul applies the Feast of Unleavened Bread to the church: "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. Therefore let us keep the feast," not with the leaven of malice but "with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth." The feast becomes a way of life for those whom Christ has delivered.

Christ's resurrection is "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep." As the first sheaf of Exodus 23:16 and 19 pledged the whole harvest to God, so Christ's rising guarantees the resurrection of "those who belong to Him" at His coming.

The Spirit was poured out "when the day of Pentecost came," the Feast of Harvest of Exodus 23:16, the Feast of Weeks. The festival of the first wheat harvest became the day of the first great harvest of the church, when about three thousand were added, Acts 2:41.

"On the last and greatest day of the feast," the Feast of Tabernacles, the later name of the Feast of Ingathering, Jesus cried out, "If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink." At the feast that celebrated God's provision of the harvest, He offered Himself as the source of living water.

"There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God." The rest of the seventh day and the seventh year pointed beyond themselves to a rest in which believers cease from their own works as God did from His, received now in Christ and completed in the age to come.

study.oneStory:
In the beginning God worked six days and rested on the seventh, and He blessed that day. After the fall, work became toil, and in Egypt it became slavery without rest. Exodus 23 answers that story. The God who rested now commands rest for His people, their servants, their animals, the foreigner and the very soil. The sabbath rhythm of creation is restored inside a redeemed community.

The passage also answers the corruption of justice that began when Cain lied about his brother and continued wherever the strong bent the truth. Israel is to be a people whose courts are straight because their God is straight, who will not follow the crowd, take a bribe or kill the innocent.

And it answers the ingratitude that marked humanity from the beginning, the refusal to glorify God as God or give thanks to Him, Romans 1:21. Three times a year all Israel would stop, travel and appear before the Lord, bringing the first and best of what He had given.

What comes after shows how hard it was to live this way. Israel's judges took bribes, the land's Sabbaths were neglected until the exile enforced them, 2 Chronicles 36:21, and the feasts were sometimes kept with hands full of offerings but hearts far from God. The law's picture of justice, rest and gratitude needed a fulfilment the law itself could not produce.

That fulfilment is Christ. At His trial every command of verses 1 to 8 was broken, and yet through that injustice God justified the wicked without bending His justice. He is our Passover, sacrificed at the Feast of Unleavened Bread; He is the firstfruits, risen from the dead; His Spirit was poured out at the Feast of Harvest; and at the Feast of Ingathering He called all who thirst to come to Him. In Him the weary find the rest the Sabbath promised, Matthew 11:28.

The story ends with the final Feast of Ingathering. A multitude "from every nation and tribe and people and tongue" stands before the throne with palm branches, Revelation 7:9, the harvest of the whole earth brought in. The Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God, Hebrews 4:9, begins in full. There will be no more false witness, no bribed judge and no weary servant, only a people gathered before the Lord, not empty-handed but carrying the praise of the Lamb.

quiz.q: What two opposite failures of justice does this chapter warn against in verses 2 to 3?

options.text: Following the crowd to pervert justice, and showing favoritism to a poor man in his lawsuit.
options.note: The text warns against bending justice in either direction, toward the majority or toward sympathy for the poor.

options.text: Only accepting bribes from the wealthy.
options.note: Bribery is addressed separately in verse 8; verses 2 to 3 specifically warn against crowd pressure and misplaced favoritism toward the poor.

options.text: Only ignoring the testimony of witnesses altogether.
options.note: The concern is bias in judgment, not simply ignoring testimony.

options.text: No warning about justice appears in this section.
options.note: Verses 2 to 3 give explicit warnings about both forms of bias.

quiz.q: What must Israelites do if they find their enemy's ox or donkey straying, according to verse 4?

options.text: Return it to him.
options.note: The command explicitly requires practical kindness even toward an enemy's property.

options.text: Keep it as compensation for past wrongs.
options.note: The text requires returning the animal, not keeping it as compensation.

options.text: Report the enemy to the judges instead.
options.note: The command is simple and direct: return the animal personally.

options.text: No instruction is given regarding an enemy's stray animal.
options.note: Verse 4 gives an explicit instruction to return it.

quiz.q: What was the purpose of letting the land rest every seventh year, according to verse 11?

options.text: So that the poor among the people could eat from the field and wild animals could consume what was left.
options.note: This social and ecological purpose is stated directly in the text.

options.text: Because the soil would otherwise become permanently infertile.
options.note: The stated reason is provision for the poor and wildlife, not a claim about permanent soil damage.

options.text: To punish landowners for prior wrongdoing.
options.note: The rest is a built-in provision for the poor, not a punitive measure.

options.text: No reason is given for the sabbatical year.
options.note: Verse 11 explicitly states the reason.

quiz.q: How many times a year were all Israel's males required to appear before the LORD, according to verse 17?

options.text: Three times a year.
options.note: The three feasts, Unleavened Bread, Harvest, and Ingathering, are explicitly named as the occasions.

options.text: Once a year, at Passover only.
options.note: The text specifies three occasions, not one.

options.text: Every single week.
options.note: Weekly Sabbath rest is commanded separately from these three annual pilgrimage feasts.

options.text: No fixed number is given.
options.note: Verse 17 explicitly states three times a year.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament connect Christ to the Feast of Harvest introduced in this chapter?

options.text: Paul calls Christ's resurrection the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.
options.note: 1 Corinthians 15:20 draws this connection directly, echoing the firstfruits language of the Feast of Harvest.

options.text: The New Testament makes no connection between Christ and any Old Testament feast.
options.note: Paul explicitly ties Christ's resurrection to firstfruits, and calls Him the Passover lamb, 1 Corinthians 5:7 and 15:20.

options.text: Jesus explicitly abolished the Feast of Harvest as meaningless.
options.note: The New Testament fulfills the feast's meaning in Christ rather than declaring it meaningless.

options.text: Only the Feast of Unleavened Bread is ever connected to Christ.
options.note: Both the Passover and the Feast of Harvest are explicitly connected to Christ in Paul's writing.

questions: This law warns against both bribery and misplaced sympathy corrupting justice. Where in your own judgments of people or situations do you notice bias creeping in from either direction, favoring the powerful or excusing the sympathetic?
Israel was commanded to help even an enemy's struggling animal. Is there someone who has wronged you that God is calling you to practically help this week, regardless of the relationship between you?

The sabbatical year built rest for the poor directly into the economic calendar, not as charity alone but as structural provision. What structures in your own life or community could better build in rest and provision for those with less?
Three times a year, Israel's whole life paused for grateful worship before God. How intentional is the rhythm of gratitude in your own calendar, or does worship only happen when it is convenient?

This chapter insists God's people be marked by both uncompromising justice and structured generosity. Which of these two, justice or generosity, comes more naturally to you, and which do you need to grow in?

translationNotes.note: Do not show favoritism to a poor man in his lawsuit balances the frequent biblical concern for the poor by insisting that a judge's role is to determine truth impartially, not to rule based on social sympathy.

The Feast of Harvest, later called the Feast of Weeks or Pentecost, and the Feast of Ingathering, later called Tabernacles or Booths, are given brief mention here and expanded in fuller detail in Leviticus 23.

You must not cook a young goat in its mother's milk is a much-discussed command; interpreters have proposed it forbids a specific pagan fertility ritual, or more broadly guards a boundary between the giving of life, milk, and the taking of it.
